meta.blurb: A painter finishes the portrait of a beautiful young man, and the young man makes a careless wish: that the picture will grow old instead of him. It comes true. As Dorian Gray stays young, his sins appear on the canvas. How long can a secret like that stay hidden?
meta.bible: Dorian Gray: a beautiful, rich young Londoner, about twenty at the start and thirty-eight at the end of the story. Basil Hallward: a kind, serious painter who paints Dorian's portrait. Lord Henry Wotton: Basil's clever, lazy friend, nicknamed Harry, who teaches Dorian to live only for pleasure. Lord Fermor: Lord Henry's old uncle. Sibyl Vane: a seventeen-year-old actress in a poor theatre, who plays Juliet and calls Dorian Prince Charming. Mrs Vane: Sibyl's faded mother. James Vane: Sibyl's younger brother, who sails away and returns to take revenge. Alan Campbell: a young chemist who was once Dorian's friend. Hetty Merton: a simple village girl whom Dorian leaves alone. Prince Charming: Sibyl's name for Dorian. Juliet: the part Sibyl plays. The portrait: the painting that grows old and cruel in place of Dorian, hidden in the old schoolroom at the top of his house. The yellow book: a French novel Lord Henry sends Dorian. London: the setting. Paris: where Basil is said to be going. Australia: where James sails. Grosvenor Gallery: a London gallery where Lord Henry says the portrait should be shown. Dorian's thirty-eighth birthday: the day after the night of the murder. Voice and tone: elegant, dark and tragic; deaths are stated plainly with no gore; the moral is that beauty without goodness is only a mask.

B1B2: In a sunny London studio full of roses, the painter Basil Hallward was finishing a portrait. His friend Lord Henry Wotton lay on a sofa, smoking, and he said that it was the best work Basil had ever done.
Basil said that he would never show the portrait, because he had put too much of himself into it. He explained that a young man named Dorian Gray had changed his art completely, as soon as they met.
Just then Dorian Gray arrived for his sitting, and Basil begged Lord Henry not to spoil him. Lord Henry only smiled and said that he would stay, because he wanted to meet this wonder.
While Basil painted, Lord Henry talked to Dorian about youth and beauty. He said that Dorian's beauty would not last, and that old age would take it away like a thief.
When the portrait was finished, Dorian stood before it and saw how beautiful he really was. Suddenly he felt a pang of sorrow, because the picture would stay young while he grew old.
Dorian cried out that he would give anything to stay young while the portrait grew old. He would even give his soul, he said, and he did not know how serious those words were.
Dorian grew angry and reached for a knife to cut the picture, but Basil held him back. In the end Basil gave him the portrait as a gift, and Dorian said he would love it forever.
Next day Lord Henry visited his old uncle, Lord Fermor, who knew everything about everyone. He learned that Dorian's mother had run away with a poor soldier, and that both his parents had died young.
Soon Dorian often visited Lord Henry's house, where his looks and his gentle voice charmed everyone. Lord Henry's ideas were exciting and dangerous, and Dorian began to believe every word of them.

One evening Dorian wandered into a poor, shabby theatre, where a young actress called Sibyl Vane played Juliet. Her voice was so lovely that he forgot everything else, and he fell in love with her at once.
Dorian met Sibyl behind the stage, and she called him Prince Charming. He told Lord Henry that they were engaged, and that he wanted his friends to see her act.
In their poor little rooms, Sibyl told her mother and her brother James about her Prince Charming. Her mother hoped that he was rich, but James was about to sail away and he was worried.
Before he left, James told his mother to watch over Sibyl and to be careful of the stranger. He swore that if the man ever hurt his sister, he would find him and punish him.
Dorian took Basil and Lord Henry to the theatre, so that they could see his future wife. But that night Sibyl acted terribly, and she spoke her lines like a lifeless doll.
Sibyl begged Dorian to understand that real love had made all her stage love seem false. But Dorian was so cruel that he said she had killed his love, and he walked out and left her crying.
Dorian walked through London all night, and at dawn he came home tired. He looked at the portrait, and he saw that a cruel line had appeared around its mouth.
Dorian hid the portrait behind a screen and wrote Sibyl a long and loving letter. He promised himself that he would marry her and live a better life from now on.
Before he could send the letter, Lord Henry arrived with terrible news. Sibyl Vane had died in the night, and Dorian cried that he had killed her.
Lord Henry told Dorian that Sibyl's death was like the last scene of a beautiful play. He said it was foolish to feel guilty, and little by little Dorian began to feel calmer.
That evening Dorian sat in a box at the opera, listening to beautiful music. He was surprised to find that he could enjoy it, and that his sorrow was already fading.
The next day Basil hurried to Dorian's house to comfort him, but he found him calm and cold. When Basil asked to see the portrait again, Dorian refused sharply and would not say why.
Dorian knew he could no longer keep the portrait in his library, where visitors might see it. He asked two workmen to carry it up to the old schoolroom at the top of the house.
In the dusty schoolroom, he set the portrait against the wall and covered it with a purple cloth. Then he locked the door and put the only key safely in his pocket.
Lord Henry sent Dorian a strange yellow book about a young man who lived only for pleasure. Dorian read it over and over, and it seemed to describe his own life.
Years passed, but Dorian's face did not change at all, even though he lived a wild life. People wondered how he could stay so fresh and pure, while others grew old around him.

People began to whisper strange stories about Dorian's secret life, and some of the young men he knew were ruined. Respectable people left the room when he came in, and old friends refused to speak to him.
Sometimes Dorian climbed the stairs to the locked room and pulled the cloth off the portrait. The face was now old and cruel, but Dorian only laughed, because he himself was still young.
Dorian filled his large house with jewels, silk, rare perfumes and strange music from many lands. He studied them with great care, hoping that beauty might help him forget what he had become.
Eighteen years after the portrait was painted, Basil met Dorian in the street late on a foggy night. Basil was leaving for Paris, but he asked to talk, and Dorian led him into the house.
Basil said that people told terrible stories about Dorian, and that several of his friends had been ruined. Dorian answered coldly that Basil did not know his life, and could not judge it.
Dorian took a lamp, led Basil upstairs to the locked room, and pulled the cloth away. Basil saw a cruel, horrible face, and he knew his own work only by the signature in the corner.
Basil fell to his knees and prayed, saying that they had both been proud and foolish. Dorian, filled with hatred for the man who had made the portrait, took a knife and killed him.
Dorian locked the door, walked downstairs, and thought carefully about what to do next. He wrote to Alan Campbell, a scientist who had once been his friend, and asked him to come.
Campbell went upstairs with his chemicals and stayed in the locked room for several hours. When he came down, no sign of Basil was left, and Dorian burned the coat and bag in the fire.
Later Dorian went back to the locked room and looked at the portrait with fear. A dark red mark had appeared on one of the painted hands, as if it were wet.
That night Dorian went to a dinner party and laughed and talked as lightly as ever. In the next days people wondered where Basil had gone, and some said he was in Paris.
Dorian could not sleep, so he went to a dark house near the river, where men went to forget their troubles. A woman there called him Prince Charming, and a sailor outside heard her speak.
James followed Dorian and caught him by the throat in the dark street. Dorian told him to look at his face under the lamp, which was no older than twenty.
After that night Dorian was very afraid, and he hardly slept at all. At a country house party, he saw James Vane's face at the glass window and nearly fainted.
The next day the guests went hunting in the woods, and Dorian walked among them. A man hidden in the bushes was shot by mistake, and the dead man was James Vane.
Dorian felt safe at last, and he promised himself that he would live a better life. Then Lord Henry told him that Alan Campbell had died by his own hand, and Dorian felt very guilty.
In a village, Dorian met a pretty girl called Hetty Merton, who was simple and innocent. Instead of harming her, he left her alone and went away, and he thought it was a good deed.
Dorian hurried to the locked room and pulled the cloth from the picture. He hoped to see a kinder face, but the eyes now looked cunning and the mouth looked false.
Dorian told Lord Henry that he wanted to be good, and that he had killed Basil. Lord Henry only laughed, and said that a gentleman like Dorian could never be a murderer.
Alone in his house, Dorian began to hate the picture, which seemed to watch his every thought. He took up the knife that had killed Basil and climbed the stairs to the locked room.
In the locked room, Dorian ran at the portrait and stabbed it with all his strength. He believed that he was killing the past, and that he would finally be free.
Two men were walking in the square outside, and they heard the terrible cry. They found a policeman and rang the bell, but at first no one inside would answer.
The servants climbed to the locked room and broke the door open. On the wall hung a splendid portrait of Dorian Gray, as young and beautiful as on the day it was painted.
On the floor in front of the picture lay a dead man in evening dress. He was old and withered, with a knife in his heart, and his face was horrible to look at.
The servants looked closely at the dead man's hands and knew him by his rings. Dorian Gray was dead, and the portrait shone down on him in all its old, pure beauty.
C1C2: On a hot summer afternoon, the studio was filled with the heavy scent of roses, and Basil Hallward stood before a tall easel, putting the last touches to a portrait of a young man of extraordinary beauty. Lord Henry Wotton, who was lying on a sofa in the corner, smoking cigarette after cigarette, declared that it was the best work Basil had ever done. He added, with his usual lazy smile, that it ought to be sent to the Grosvenor Gallery at once.

Basil answered, with a sudden flush, that he would never exhibit it, because he had put too much of himself into the painting and feared that the world would see his secret. Lord Henry laughed at this, but Basil insisted that he had met the young man, Dorian Gray, at a party, and that from that moment his whole art had been changed. Dorian, he said, was no longer a model, but the very idea of beauty that a painter spends his life looking for, and he could not bear to share him.

At that moment Dorian Gray was announced, a young man with golden hair, rosy lips and clear blue eyes, who looked so open and innocent that people trusted him at once. Basil begged his friend not to influence him, for Dorian had a beautiful nature, and a bad word might ruin it, but Lord Henry only smiled, saying that he would never do such a thing. Then Basil, who could not resist, asked him to stay, and Lord Henry settled again on his sofa to meet the wonder he had heard so much about.

In the garden, Lord Henry spoke to Dorian in a low, musical voice, and every word seemed to open a door in the young man's mind that had never been opened before. He told him that youth is the one thing worth having, that beauty is a kind of genius, and that some day, when his face was lined and his hair grey, Dorian would feel it all slip away. Dorian listened in silence, troubled by a sudden fear, while the bees moved among the flowers and the afternoon grew quiet around them.

When at last Basil put down his brush, Dorian stood before the portrait and, for the first time, saw how beautiful he was, and he flushed with a pleasure that was almost pain. Then the words of Lord Henry came back to him, and he understood with sudden clarity that he would one day be old and wrinkled, while the painting would remain young forever. The thought struck him like a knife, and his eyes filled with bitter, helpless tears of grief.

In a voice shaking with grief and envy, Dorian cried out that he would give everything he possessed to stay young, if only the portrait could grow old in his place. He would give his soul for it, he said, and he spoke in the heat of the moment, without understanding what such words might mean. In the quiet studio nobody answered, and nothing seemed to change, although something had perhaps begun.

Dorian blamed Basil for making a picture that would mock him in his old age, and he snatched a long knife from the table, as if to slash the canvas, but the painter seized his hand and pulled him away. Basil said that he had painted it for Dorian, and that it was his own, and he promised to have it framed and sent to his house. Dorian, ashamed of his outburst, thanked him warmly, and Lord Henry watched it all with the calm curiosity of a man who has lit a fire and wants to see how it will burn.

The next morning Lord Henry called on his uncle, Lord Fermor, an old gentleman who knew every family in London and was never tired of talking about them. He learned that Dorian's mother had been a famous beauty who ran away with a poor young soldier, and that her father had taken the child, after both parents had died. Lord Henry thought the story romantic, and he resolved to make this beautiful, lonely boy into a creature of his own design.

Within a few weeks Dorian was seen everywhere with Lord Henry, and wherever he went, people marvelled at his beauty and the sweetness of his manners. Lord Henry filled his mind with new, daring ideas, which taught him that pleasure was the only thing worth pursuing and that conscience was a kind of cowardice. Dorian, who was young, rich and eager to feel everything, drank in these doctrines as thirstily as he drank the wine of the table.

One evening Dorian wandered through the grey, crowded streets and stepped into a dingy little theatre, where a young actress named Sibyl Vane was playing Juliet before a rough, restless audience. She was barely seventeen, with a face like a flower and a voice like music, and from the moment she first spoke, Dorian forgot the theatre, the crowd and the whole world. He saw her night after night, and he told himself that he had never been truly happy until he found her.

After the play Dorian went to Sibyl and told her that he loved her, and she, who did not even know his name, called him Prince Charming, because he seemed to her the hero of a fairy tale. He rushed to tell Lord Henry that they were engaged, and Lord Henry, who thought the whole affair delightful but foolish, said that it was a pity to marry a woman one had admired on the stage. Dorian, though, would hear nothing against her, and he invited both Lord Henry and Basil to the theatre to see her.

In the shabby rooms where she lived with her mother and her younger brother, Sibyl spoke of her Prince Charming with shining eyes, though she could not tell them his real name. Her mother, a faded actress who always lived in the past, thought only of whether the stranger was wealthy, while James, a gloomy, rough-mannered boy who was about to sail for Australia, loved his sister too deeply to be easy. He asked who this man was, and the more she praised him, the more uneasy he became.

On the day he left for the ship, James took his mother aside and made her promise to watch over Sibyl, and he said bitterly that no gentleman ever truly cared for an actress. He swore, with a face dark with fury, that if the man ever did her harm, he would hunt him down and make him pay. Then he sailed away, carrying that anger across the sea, and Sibyl was left alone with her happiness and her mother.

Dorian brought Basil and Lord Henry to the dingy theatre in triumph, certain that they would worship her as he did, but that night Sibyl was dreadful. She spoke her lines in a flat, empty voice and moved like a puppet, and her stiff, false gestures made the audience laugh and hiss. Dorian, pale with shame, sat motionless, while Lord Henry said calmly that the girl was lovely but could not act, and Basil suggested they leave.

Dorian went behind the stage and found her radiant, and she explained that she had always played at love, until real love had shown her how false and empty the stage was. He told her coldly that she had killed his love, that without her art she was nothing, and that he could never see her again, and he left while she lay weeping on the floor. He did not look back, though she stretched out her hands to him, and he felt no pity at all.

He wandered through the streets until dawn, passing sleeping markets and silent houses, and when he came home he stood in his library and noticed that the portrait looked different. Around the mouth of the painted face was a faint line of cruelty, as though the picture had taken on the shape of what he had done to Sibyl. Terrified, he rubbed his eyes, and then he understood that his wish in Basil's studio had come true, and that the picture, not he, would pay for his sins.

Dorian drew a heavy screen across the picture, unable to look at it, and sat down to write a letter in which he begged Sibyl's forgiveness and called himself a brute. He swore that he would marry her, that he would be good from now on, and that nothing in the world should ever separate him from her again. For the first time in his life, he felt that the real Dorian, not the painted one, had a chance to be better.

Before the letter was sent, Lord Henry arrived with a grave face and told him that Sibyl Vane was dead, and that she had taken her own life the night before. Dorian cried out that he had murdered her, that he was a monster, and that it was the cruelest thing that had ever happened to him. Lord Henry would not let him blame himself, and he said that it was a sad accident and that it was best not to dwell on it.

Lord Henry sat by him and spoke softly, saying that the girl had lived and died like a heroine of tragedy and had therefore achieved something far finer than ordinary life. He argued that sorrow is a kind of passion, that remorse is merely a form of vanity, and that it was better to take such things as a work of art than as a sin on the conscience. Slowly Dorian felt the weight lifting from him, and he was ashamed that he found it so easy.

That evening, as Lord Henry advised, Dorian went to the opera, and as the music rose and fell around him he sat in his box and thought of how little his own grief seemed to weigh. The more he listened, the more he realised that Sibyl's death had become for him a distant tragedy that he could watch from his seat as if it belonged to a stranger. At last he laughed softly at himself, and he did not feel guilty at all.

The next day Basil hurried to Dorian's house to comfort him, only to find him sitting calmly at breakfast, and it shocked him that Dorian could speak of Sibyl's death as though it were a play he had seen. When Basil, who had come to offer the strength of an old friendship, asked to see the portrait once more, Dorian cried out that he must never look at it. Basil was so surprised and hurt by the refusal that he left, and Dorian was left alone with his secret and a growing fear.

Dorian realised that he could no longer leave the portrait in the library, where any visitor might see it, and he resolved to hide it in the old schoolroom at the top of the house. Two workmen came, and they carried the great frame up the stairs, wrapped in a cover of heavy cloth, grumbling at its weight and wondering what it contained. Dorian kept his hand on the banister the whole way, as pale as paper.

The room was dusty, silent and full of old toys, and there Dorian set the portrait against the wall and covered it with a purple cloth, so that no eye but his own might ever see what it had become. He locked the door behind him, put the only key in his pocket, and walked slowly downstairs, thinking that he was safe, though he knew that the picture would grow older while he would not. It would grow as old as sin, but Dorian Gray would remain a youth, and he told himself it was a bargain worth keeping.

Lord Henry sent him a strange yellow book, about a young Parisian who tried to live every passion and every pleasure that the world had ever known. Dorian read it greedily, again and again, until it seemed to him that it described his own life before he had lived it, and that its poisonous beauty had been written for him alone. He kept it beside him for years, and he tried to live as its hero had lived.

Year followed year, and Dorian Gray plunged into every pleasure that London could offer, yet his face remained as smooth and fresh as on the day Basil had painted him. His friends grew grey, his enemies grew stout, but Dorian, with his golden hair and clear eyes, seemed to be untouched by time. People marvelled that so innocent a face could belong to a man of whom such stories were told.

Rumours began to circulate about the places where he spent his nights and the company he kept, and some of the young men who had admired him were found ruined, disgraced or dead. Respectable people left the room when he came in, and at his club men turned away, but Dorian only smiled, for he had a charm that most people could not resist. Still, those who looked into his bright, innocent eyes found it hard to believe the stories.

Sometimes, late at night, Dorian climbed the stairs to the locked room, drew the cloth from the portrait, and looked at the face that was growing coarser and more cruel with every sin. He studied the wrinkles that gathered around its eyes and the heavy, sensual mouth, and he compared them with his own flawless reflection in the glass. Then he would laugh, a little wildly, and cover the picture again, and go downstairs as lovely and untroubled as a boy.

He filled his great house with rare treasures, with jewels that glittered like cold fire, tapestries woven by forgotten hands, strange instruments from distant lands and perfumes that stirred memories he had never lived. For years he studied these things as if they were a language, hoping that beauty might drown the voice of his conscience, and that some new sensation might finally satisfy him. But the satisfaction never lasted, and each new passion left him as restless as before.

One foggy November night, the eve of Dorian's thirty-eighth birthday, Basil Hallward, on his way to Paris, stopped him in front of his house, and said that he must speak with him at once. Dorian, who was tired and in no mood for talk, declared that he would give Basil half an hour, but he led him into the library and poured himself a glass of wine with a careless air. Basil settled in a chair, with the look of a man who has made up his mind, and began to speak.

Basil told him gravely that London was full of ugly stories, that several young men who had been Dorian's companions were now ruined or disgraced, and that he could not reconcile such a reputation with such a face. Dorian only shrugged and said that it was not for Basil to judge him, since a man who knows only one half of another's life can say nothing about the other half. Basil answered that he must see his soul, and Dorian, with a sudden wild idea, said that he should see it too.

Dorian led the way up the stairs with a lamp in his hand and, in the cold, dusty room, tore the purple cloth from the picture, saying that Basil had wanted to see his soul, and that now he should. The face on the canvas was a hideous thing, twisted by years of cruelty and vice, and Basil recognised his own work only by the signature at the corner and by the faint outline of the youth he had loved. Basil cried that it must be a trick or a joke of the devil, and he stared in horror at the thing he had made.

Basil sank to his knees before the picture and began to pray, begging God to forgive them both for their pride and their foolishness. At that moment Dorian felt an overwhelming hatred of the man who had painted the portrait, who had caused all his troubles, and he caught up a knife that lay on the table and struck. It was over in a few seconds, and Dorian stood very still, listening to the silence of the house.

Without a sound, Dorian locked the door, went downstairs, and sat for a long time looking at the fire, thinking coldly of what he must do. He remembered Alan Campbell, a young chemist and a once-close friend who had long since turned away from him, and he wrote to him, asking him to come at once. When Campbell arrived, white and stern, Dorian told him, with terrible calm, what he needed, and when Campbell refused, he forced him with a secret that could ruin him.

Campbell, grey with horror and shame, took his chemicals upstairs and worked for several hours in the locked room, and when he came down at last, he said nothing but that it was done. After that he went away without a word, and Dorian never saw him again, though he thought of him for a long time. Then Dorian burned Basil's coat and bag, and nothing was left to show that his old friend had ever come.

Later, when the house was quiet, Dorian climbed the stairs again and looked at the portrait, and he felt a terrible curiosity to see whether it showed what he had done. A dark red stain lay across one of the painted hands, wet and shining, as if the canvas itself had remembered the crime, and the face seemed to be smiling at him with a cruel pleasure. He hurried out, locked the door, and tried to tell himself that it meant nothing at all.

That very evening Dorian dressed carefully and went to a brilliant dinner party, where he laughed and talked with such ease that nobody there could have guessed what he had done a few hours before. In the following days, people began to ask where Basil Hallward had gone, and some said that he had been seen in Paris, while others spoke of detectives and the police. Dorian read the newspapers with a calm face, but he did not feel safe in his own house any longer.

Haunted by what he had done, Dorian went one night to a low, dark house near the docks, where men lay in a haze of smoke, trying to forget the world. As he was leaving, a woman called out to him, using the old name Prince Charming, which Sibyl had given him, and a sailor outside the door turned sharply at the words. It was James Vane, who had returned from Australia after eighteen years, and who had sworn that he would find the man who had ruined his sister.

James followed him into the street, seized him by the throat and cried that he would kill him, but Dorian, with great presence of mind, told him to look at his face under the lamp. James saw only the smooth, bright face of a boy of twenty, and he let him go, shaken, murmuring that he must be wrong, since the man who ruined his sister had wronged her eighteen years before. Then a woman ran after him and told him that the young man had sold his soul for beauty, and that he had looked the same eighteen years ago.

After that night Dorian lived in terror, for he knew that James Vane would not give up, and he trembled at every sound in the street. A few days later, at a house party in the country, he was standing in the conservatory with Lord Henry and a lady when he saw, pressed against the glass, the dark face of the sailor watching him. He cried out and almost fainted, and when his friends asked what was wrong, he could only say that he was ill.

The next morning the guests went out shooting in the woods, and Dorian, uneasy and pale, kept close to the others, although he felt that a watching eye was following him everywhere. A shot was fired, a cry was heard, and the party found that a man hidden in the bushes had been hit by accident, and that he was dead. When Dorian looked at the dead face, he saw that it was James Vane, and he felt relief so sudden and great that he nearly wept.

Dorian told himself that the danger had passed forever, and he declared that from now on he would be a better man, and leave the old sins behind him. His fresh vows were shaken, however, when Lord Henry mentioned casually that Alan Campbell had been found dead, by his own hand, and Dorian felt a cold shiver that he could not explain. He thought of the terrible night in the locked room, and he knew that the past was not so easily forgotten.

In a quiet country village, Dorian met a simple, pretty girl named Hetty Merton, who thought him a gentleman and a good man, and he felt a strange pleasure in the thought of her innocence. Instead of doing her the harm he had done to others, he decided to leave her alone and go back to London, and he told himself that this was his first good action in many years. For a moment he almost believed that he had truly changed, and that a better life was still possible for him.

Excited by his own goodness, Dorian hurried to the locked room and tore the cloth from the picture, expecting to find that the face had grown a little gentler. Instead he found only the same cruel features, now touched by a sly and hypocritical smile, and he understood that his action had been done from vanity and curiosity rather than from love. He covered his eyes, ashamed, and he knew that nothing in the picture could change unless he himself changed.

Dorian visited Lord Henry and confessed that he wished to lead a better life, and then, in a tone that shook with emotion, he said that he had killed Basil Hallward. Lord Henry laughed lightly, as at a good joke, and answered that crime was for the common people, and that Dorian was too refined and too fond of beauty ever to commit such a deed. The words made Dorian feel stranger and lonelier than ever, for even the one man who knew him best would not believe him.

When Lord Henry had gone, Dorian sat alone and began to hate the portrait, for it had been his conscience, and it was the only witness to all his sins. If it were gone, he thought, he would be free of the past, and he would be able to live in peace as he had never lived before. Seizing the knife that had killed Basil, he climbed the stairs once more, like a man about to break a chain.

In the cold schoolroom, he stood in front of the evil, shining face and raised the knife, believing that if he killed the picture he would kill the past, and that its dreadful life would die with it. He struck at the canvas with all his strength, and the room was filled with a terrible cry and the sound of something heavy falling. Then there was a long silence, and the whole great house seemed to hold its breath and listen.

Outside, in the foggy square, two men who were passing stopped and looked up at the great house, which had suddenly become silent, and one of them went off to find a policeman. When they returned, they rang the bell and knocked, but no answer came, for the house was dark except for one light in an upper window, and it seemed asleep. At last, after a long wait, the servants awoke, trembling and pale, and came down in their nightclothes to ask what was wrong.

The servants and the policeman climbed the stairs together, and at last, after repeated attempts, they forced the door of the locked room, and held up their lamps. On the wall hung a magnificent portrait of their master, as he had appeared in the first splendour of his youth and beauty, without a mark or a blemish. It was so lovely that for a moment they simply stood and stared, unable to say a word.

On the floor in front of the picture lay a dead man in evening dress, with a knife in his heart, and he was withered, wrinkled and loathsome of face, a terrible contrast to the lovely portrait above him. None of the servants had ever seen the man, and they could not believe that so ugly a creature had been in their master's house. They drew nearer in silence, afraid to touch him, and they wondered who he could be.

At last the servants looked more closely at the hands of the dead man, and by the rings that glittered upon his fingers they knew that it was their master, Dorian Gray. Thus the wish made in a sunlit studio so many years before had been paid for in full, and the picture that had borne his sins now hung on the wall, as young and lovely as ever. It was a warning that no one can escape the story written on his own soul, and that beauty without goodness is only a mask.
